source: Gentner & Markman (1994) Structural alignment in comparison: no difference without similarity
finding: Core test of the 'no difference without similarity' claim. People list differences for MORE word pairs when the pairs are similar, and the extra differences are almost all alignable ones. Nonalignable differences do not change with similarity.
numbers: Exp 1 (32 listers, 40 pairs, 5-min limit, 'do the easiest pairs first'): similar pairs M=11.44 vs dissimilar M=5.88 pairs with a difference listed, F(1,30)=31.88, p<.001. Alignable differences 8.97 vs 3.88, F(1,30)=31.37, p<.001. Nonalignable 2.47 vs 2.00, F(1,30)=1.39, ns. Similarity norms came from 40 other undergraduates.
quote: it should be easier to find the differences between pairs of similar items than between pairs of dissimilar items
limits: Word pairs of concrete nouns, undergraduates, one difference per pair. Alignability coded by two raters (97% initial agreement).
agent_relevance: S2 compare: two near-matching candidates make the decisive difference easy to see. Two far-apart candidates yield few usable differences, so pair by similarity first.

source: Gentner & Markman (1994) Structural alignment in comparison: no difference without similarity
finding: Between-subjects version of the same effect. It rules out the objection that people just picked easy (similar) pairs first, or spent more time on the interesting pairs.
numbers: Exp 2 (48 subjects; 24 saw only similar pairs, 24 only dissimilar): pairs with a difference listed 18.42 vs 13.79, t(46)=2.69, p<.01. Alignable 15.63 vs 11.54, t(46)=2.06, p<.05. Nonalignable 2.79 vs 2.25, ns.
limits: Effect is modest in Exp 2 (about 4.6 pairs). Word-pair listing only, not reasoning or decisions.
agent_relevance: The effect is not a strategy artefact, which supports building S2 around a matched pair.

source: Gentner & Markman (1994) Structural alignment in comparison: no difference without similarity
finding: Competing explanation checked: a 'narrow strategy' account (people pick a few easy kinds of difference for similar pairs). The type analysis does not support it.
numbers: The most common difference types for low-similarity pairs made up 76% of listed differences; for high-similarity pairs only 62%. Similar pairs gave a wider range of differences, not a narrower one.
limits: Post hoc tabulation, not a designed test.
agent_relevance: Similar pairs give richer, more varied differences, so a near-pair comparison should not be expected to give a narrow set.

source: Markman & Gentner (1993) All differences are not created equal: a structural alignment view of similarity (CogSci proceedings)
finding: Earlier conference version of the same two experiments. Same pattern: alignable differences scale with pair similarity, nonalignable do not.
numbers: Exp 1 (32 undergraduates): 11.38 vs 5.88 pairs; alignable 9.09 vs 3.88, t(31)=5.62; nonalignable 2.28 vs 2.00, ns. Exp 2 (48): 18.42 vs 13.63 pairs, t(46)=2.75; alignable 15.63 vs 11.38, t(46)=2.13; nonalignable 2.79 vs 2.25, t(46)=0.47. All tests one-tailed. A response-time version was only a pilot.
limits: Proceedings paper. Means differ slightly from the 1994 journal version (11.38 vs 11.44, 13.63 vs 13.79). Its Table 1 repeats Exp 1 values for Exp 2 (a printing error).
agent_relevance: Quote the 1994 numbers. This paper confirms the design and that the effect was found twice.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: The 1997 American Psychologist review states the alignment account and adds a similarity-judgment test: a difference that is alignable lowers perceived similarity more than the same contrast presented as nonalignable.
numbers: Forced-choice triad (arrow at a bird vs arrow at a target with a bird beside it): participants chose the nonalignable-difference picture as more similar (Markman & Gentner 1996, Memory & Cognition). Counts are in the original paper, not this review.
limits: Review; triad numbers not given here. Rests on a few picture sets.
agent_relevance: When an agent scores how close two options are, a gap on a shared dimension should weigh more than a stray extra feature.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Candidate inferences follow the alignment: facts connected to the matched structure carry over, unconnected facts do not (Clement & Gentner 1991). Choice research shows the same split: alignable differences get more weight in decisions.
numbers: Cited: video-game choice justifications held more alignable than nonalignable differences (Markman & Medin 1995). Jacket and calculator example (Kahneman & Tversky 1984): a $5 saving was judged worth a trip when it was a large share of the cheap item's price (calculator 15 to 10) but not of the dear item's (jacket 125 to 120).
limits: Secondhand summary of other studies; sample sizes not shown here.
agent_relevance: Transfer is licensed by the matched structure. In S2, copy a conclusion across only if it hangs on the part that matched.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: The authors answer the 'similarity is not enough' objection (theory-based categorisation, e.g. bats and birds) by saying that structural alignment brings relations and theory knowledge into the similarity computation itself. They name ACME (Holyoak & Thagard) and Copycat (Hofstadter) as rival or complementary mapping mechanisms.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Theoretical argument. It does not test the rival theories against each other.
agent_relevance: Warns against equating 'compare' with surface overlap. The comparison step should use relations.

source: Loewenstein & Gentner (2005) Relational language and the development of relational mapping
finding: Relational language boosts children's relational mapping. Preschoolers who heard spatial words (top, middle, bottom) found the hidden 'winner' in a three-tier box more often than children who did not.
numbers: Exp 1, neutral objects, 3;8-year-olds: 72% correct with language vs 45% baseline, F(1,84)=9.53, p<.005. 4;1-year-olds: 71% vs 64%, ns. 61% of language children were above chance (33%) vs 20% of baseline.
limits: Spatial terms, 3-5 year-olds, one mapping game. The older group already did well (ceiling).
agent_relevance: Giving the agent explicit relation words (for example 'is the larger of', 'is caused by') before it compares may sharpen the match. Test this.

source: Loewenstein & Gentner (2005) Relational language and the development of relational mapping
finding: The language effect appears at older ages when the task is harder (cross-mapped, where the object lure points to the wrong tier).
numbers: Exp 3 (60 children): 4;7-year-olds 65% language vs 45% baseline, F(1,54)=4.05, p<.05. 5;2-year-olds 73% vs 53%. 4;1-year-olds 32% vs 28%, ns. 70% of language children vs 47% of baseline were above chance.
limits: Small cells. Many errors were object-lure errors.
agent_relevance: Relational help matters most when surface cues mislead. This is the reason to compare in the schema: to beat tempting surface matches.

source: Loewenstein & Gentner (2005) Relational language and the development of relational mapping
finding: The words must fit the relation, and the gain lasts.
numbers: Exp 4: top-middle-bottom 62% correct vs on-in-under 40%, F(1,44)=13.31, p<.005; at 4;2 years 67% vs 35%, at 3;7 57% vs 44% (ns). Exp 5: children kept an advantage over baseline when retested 2 days later without hearing the words again.
limits: Retention shown for one task over 2 days.
agent_relevance: Label choice matters. Pick relation names that match the structure you want found.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: Analogical encoding in adults: comparing two cases beats studying them one at a time. Replicated across three experiments with negotiation cases.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=64): trade-off solutions 59% (compare) vs 22% (separate), chi2(1)=8.26, p<.01. Contingent contracts 38% vs 16%, chi2(1,N=64)=3.92, p<.05. Full schema stated by 42% of comparers. Exp 3 (N=158): contingent contracts in face-to-face negotiation 90% guided analogy, 70% compare, 55% separate cases, 37% no training.
limits: Negotiation scripts, undergraduates; outcome is strategy use in a new case. Some comparers still needed prompting to write the principle.
agent_relevance: Strong human case for S2: have the model compare two worked examples and write the shared rule, instead of reading them in turn. Gain was 2-3 times.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: A dose-response: more comparison support gave more transfer. The bare instruction to compare helped, guided analogy (with definition and diagrams) helped most.
numbers: Exp 3 (N=158; 40 per condition, 38 baseline): 37% none < 55% separate < 70% compare < 90% guided. Ideal contract suggested: 73% guided and 68% compare vs 48% separate and 47% baseline, chi2(1,N=158)=8.30, p<.01.
limits: Pairs negotiated, so partners' ideas are blended.
agent_relevance: A bare 'compare these' is weaker than 'compare, then state the common rule and map the parts'. Supply structure when the model compares.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: Schema abstraction is the mechanism: comparers wrote fuller statements of the common principle than separate-case learners.
numbers: Exp 3: 35% of comparers fully articulated the schema vs 8% of separate-case learners. Exp 1: 44% of guided contingent-contract analogy participants proposed a contingent contract vs almost none in the other two conditions (1 of 16 in trade-off analogy, 0 baseline).
limits: Schema scores hand-coded (about 93% coder agreement on solutions).
agent_relevance: Make the agent write the common principle as an explicit short rule after comparing, and store it.

source: Kurtz, Miao & Gentner (2001) Learning by analogical bootstrapping
finding: Mutual alignment of two half-understood cases (heat flow scenarios) teaches the common causal structure, but only when the comparison is intensive.
numbers: N=80 adults, 20 per condition (control, separate interpretation, joint interpretation, joint interpretation plus listing correspondences). Causal relevance of listed differences F(3,76)=2.75, p<.05; only Joint+Corr differed from control (Dunnett p<.05). Similarity rating F(3,76)=4.42, p<.05. Proportion of alignable differences F(3,76)=1.33, p>.10 (ns). Descriptions including the schema F(3,76)=2.09, p about .10 (trend, Joint+Corr M=6.3).
limits: The alignable-proportion prediction did not reach significance; the authors blame strict coding. Weak manipulations (seeing both scenarios, or separate interpretation) gave no reliable gain.
agent_relevance: Light-touch comparison may do nothing. S2 should require explicit correspondence listing (A1 maps to B1), not just 'look at both'.

source: Kurtz, Miao & Gentner (2001) Learning by analogical bootstrapping
finding: Experiment 2 isolates what helps: making correspondences. Joint interpretation plus correspondences beat correspondences alone.
numbers: Correct correspondences, Joint+Corr vs correspondence-only: t(9)=2.684, p<.05 (about 10 per group).
limits: Very small groups.
agent_relevance: Interpreting both together and listing correspondences appear additive. Do both in S2.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction
finding: Children aged 5-7 learn a spatial principle (diagonal braces make buildings stable) better from highly alignable pairs, and also from a contrastive label. Replicates the earlier alignability effect.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=64, 16 per cell, 2x2 alignability x label): repair task braces placed 78% high-alignment vs 41% low; transfer 84% vs 53%; label 88% vs no label 50%. Label could not affect repair (given afterwards): 62% vs 56%. Exp 2 (N=116, 29 per cell, power analysis planned): Day 2 near transfer high 95% vs low 56%; label 88% vs control 63%. Far construction: label 40% vs 21%, no alignability effect (36% vs 24%). Far recognition: 72% vs 52%; label 74% vs 54%. Effects held after 2-5 days.
limits: Children only, one spatial principle. In Exp 1 the test of whether the alignability advantage differed with the label was not significant (p=.70). Boys outscored girls on some tasks (transfer .83 vs .57, p=.034). 15 children lost in Exp 2 for not returning.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'comparison plus a name for the key difference'. Naming the found difference (for example 'diagonal beam') may help the agent carry it forward.

source: Richland & Zhao (2026) Relational reasoning and educational applications (review)
finding: Teaching review: put aligned pairs side by side so the key alignable difference stands out. It helps only when learners have some prior knowledge.
numbers: Hansen & Richland (2020): mitosis and meiosis side by side beat one at a time, though side by side loads memory more. Rittle-Johnson et al. (2009): algebra learners who already tried moving terms across the equals sign learned better from simultaneous comparison; those with no starting skill learned better from separate study. Richland & McDonough (2010): high-cuing video condition gave more positive extension and less capture by misleading context, immediately and after one week.
limits: Secondary summary; effect sizes not given in this text.
agent_relevance: Moderator for S2: comparing two cases helps when the agent has some grasp of the domain. With none, give separate worked examples first.

source: Richland & Zhao (2026) Relational reasoning and educational applications (review)
finding: Visual alignment makes discrepancies visible. Simultaneous presentation can help noticing (X-ray reading, Kok et al. 2013) and learning in games (Bustamante et al. 2022).
numbers: Kok et al. (2013), as cited: two X-rays matched in all surface features except one key difference let people find the discrepancy easily. Bustamante et al. (2022): showing conversion problems together raised learning and transfer, but depended on prior knowledge.
limits: Secondhand. Not an LLM result.
agent_relevance: Present two candidate solutions in the same format and order, so the relevant gap is the only gap.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review (Educational Psychologist 48, 87-113)
finding: Meta-analysis of case-comparison instruction. Seen by title in the Richland 2026 reference list only; the paper was not opened (the Northwestern URL returned an HTML error page).
numbers: Not verified. No numbers recorded; I recall an overall positive effect of about half a standard deviation but did not read it this session.
limits: Do not cite numbers without opening the paper.
agent_relevance: Would be the best effect-size anchor for S2. Fetch it in a later pass.

source: Critics of alignment: 'On the necessity of alignment: reply to Costello and Keane (2001)' (JEP:LMC 27, 272); 'The importance of being nonalignable: a critical test of the structural alignment theory of similarity' (JEP:LMC 30(5), 1082, 2004)
finding: Titles in a Europe PMC listing show that rival accounts disputed whether alignment is necessary for similarity, and that a 2004 paper built a critical test around nonalignable differences. Contents not opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only titles seen. Do not infer the direction of the result.
agent_relevance: Flag: the alignment account has direct critics. Review before treating it as settled.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text analogy tasks, but on story analogies, the closest to Gentner-style cross-domain comparison, people did better.
numbers: Digit matrices: N=40 humans; GPT-3 above human mean, OR=1.88, p=.005, 95% CI [1.21, 2.91] (generation); OR=6.27 for choosing from options. Letter strings: N=57; zero-generalization OR=1.76, p=.0007. Story analogies (N=54, Gentner et al. materials): GPT-3 picked the causally matching story p=.0005 overall, near analogy p=.0039, far analogy p=.065 (ns); humans significant in both; humans better, OR=0.37, p=.0003. 15 of 54 people chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-4 (preliminary, ChatGPT interface, 72 problems) near-perfect on near and strong on far.
limits: Single model; training-data overlap not excluded (disputed by Hodel & West). GPT-4 result is a preliminary check.
agent_relevance: Baseline: LLMs can pick a relationally matched story over a surface-matched one, but far (cross-domain) mapping was the weak spot of GPT-3. Do not assume the comparison step is flawless.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Qualitative test with the radiation problem (Gick & Holyoak): GPT-3 alone failed, but given the general-and-fortress source story it found the convergence solution.
numbers: Qualitative only, no counts.
limits: One problem. Not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: One good analogue can turn a failed attempt into a success. This is the use case for retrieving a source example in S2.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Robustness check of the Webb et al. results. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 do worse than humans when problems keep the abstract rule but change surface form.
numbers: Digit matrices (human n=1,550 digit problems): humans .715 digits, .771 alternate blank position, .704 symbols. The GPT models score about .81 on standard digits but about .48 when the blank moves. The extracted table is garbled, so which of GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 has which row is uncertain. Letter strings: humans stay stable across alphabets; GPT models drop sharply, most with symbol alphabets.
limits: Prolific samples; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (0613); table text extraction imperfect.
agent_relevance: Surface changes break LLM analogy more than human analogy. A scaffold should re-test a found match on a rewritten version of the problem (G3).

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogies show answer-order bias in GPT-4 and a larger loss from paraphrase than for people.
numbers: WHL's GPT-4: 89% (16/18) when the correct story came first vs 61% (11/18) second. In this paper's re-run, GPT-4 shows the same bias; humans show none (about .78 either way, 292/373 vs 272/347). Paraphrasing the correct story: GPT-4 .86 (31/36) to .72 (26/36); humans .78 (564/720) to .70 (503/720). 18 far-analogy stories; the difference in drop not tested as significant.
limits: Only 18 stories. Table row labels are scrambled in the extract, so the 89/61 figures from the prose are the reliable ones.
agent_relevance: Position bias in pairwise comparison is real. Randomise and swap A/B order in code (guardrail G5).

source: Hodel & West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalisation of the original claim: modified letter-string problems (a shuffled synthetic alphabet and two-letter intervals) drop GPT-3 to near zero while humans stay high.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy below 0.1 on four modified transformation types (extend sequence, successor, predecessor, fix alphabetic sequence) with the synthetic alphabet; only 'remove redundant letter' and 'sort' stayed near the original range. Human performance 'remains at a level similar across modifications'.
limits: Authors argue human tests may not measure LLMs. Webb et al. replied that counting is the weak point and that a code-running GPT-4 solved shuffled-alphabet variants (as reported by Lewis & Mitchell).
agent_relevance: A rival explanation: analogical success may rest on familiar content. Test with tool-assisted counting and unfamiliar symbols.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2024/2025) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Generalising an analogy rule across alphabets: children and adults carry the rule across Latin, Greek and symbol alphabets; LLMs lose accuracy as the alphabet becomes less familiar.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin / Greek / Symbol: adults (n=62) .88/.91/.89; children aged 7-9 (n=41) .62/.66/.67; GPT-4o (54 runs) .85/.63/.48; Llama-3.1 405B .79/.74/.27; Claude-3.5 .68/.62/.46; Gemma-2 27B .60/.39/.14. Latin-to-Greek drop significant for each model (Bonferroni p<.001, Llama p=.012).
limits: Letter strings only. Claude-3.5 and Gemma-2 did worse than children even in Latin.
agent_relevance: Even strong models lose the relational rule when the tokens change. This is the main weakness S2 must guard against.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Analogical prompting: ask the model to recall 3-5 distinct relevant problems it writes itself, solve them, then solve the real one. Beats zero-shot chain of thought and often manual few-shot chain of thought.
numbers: Average gain +4% across tasks. GSM8K, GPT-3.5-turbo: 5-shot CoT 75.0%, self-generated variants 75.8-77.8% (table rows misaligned in extract). Exemplar count: K=1 76.1 GSM8K / 34.8 MATH; K=3 or 5 about 77.3-77.8 / 37.0-37.3. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5-turbo 15% vs GPT-4 16% with self-generated knowledge plus exemplars. Manual check of 100 GSM8K/MATH solved items: of 50 correct, 35 had relevant correct exemplars, 6 irrelevant, 9 relevant but wrong.
limits: This is analogical retrieval, not comparison of two cases: the model does not align examples against the target. Gains are small. K=1 underperformed because one exemplar dominates.
agent_relevance: Weak but positive. Self-generated examples help, but one is brittle. Use at least 2-3 distinct ones, then compare them (not tested in this paper).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Model strength moderates the effect: self-generated analogies pay off only when the model can produce correct, relevant exemplars.
numbers: text-davinci-003 GSM8K: 5-shot CoT 14.8% vs 50.3% to 61.0% for self-generation variants as extracted. For models weaker than text-davinci-002, manual few-shot CoT beat self-generated exemplars.
limits: Extracted table partly garbled. Check Table 1 before quoting the davinci numbers.
agent_relevance: On a weaker model, do not rely on self-made examples. Supply vetted examples from a bank.
